title: Profitable but broke
setting: An owner and her accountant look at why cash is tight.

lines.t: We had our best year, and I nearly couldn't pay salaries in November.
That's not a profit problem. That's cash flow.
The profit margin held at nineteen per cent.
And accounts receivable is thirty-four thousand, most of it overdue.
Two clients treat sixty days as a suggestion.
Then ask for thirty per cent upfront on every new contract.
Won't that scare people off?
Some will push back. Almost nobody actually leaves.
And the ones already late?
Chase on day thirty-one, not day sixty-one. A short polite email.

title: The quote was too low
setting: Reviewing a project that came in under the break-even point.

lines.t: We made a three per cent margin. Our break-even point is twelve.
I know. The pages took three times longer than normal text.
Did we see a sample before quoting?
No. The client said the budget was tight, so I ran the numbers quickly.
And discounted fifteen per cent before knowing the scope.
Yes. They accepted the same day, which should have warned me.
It usually does. Let's make one rule from this.
No quote without a sample of the real material.
And no discount before the scope is clear.
Agreed. I'll put it in the template so nobody forgets.

title: Profitable and empty
setting: The accounts show a profit and the bank account disagrees.

lines.t: We're profitable and the bank account is empty.
Profit and cash flow are two different stories, and yours are three months apart.
How bad is it?
You're 14% over budget on overheads, and the rent went up in January.
Rent is a fixed cost. I can't touch it.
The variable costs are where you have choices. Deliveries, packaging, overtime.
Give me a ballpark figure. How much has to go?
Eleven thousand a month. Run the numbers yourself tonight and you'll reach the same figure.
So we tighten the belt until June.
Until the March invoices land. Cut costs where customers never see it, and stop discounting to win work you can't finance.
That last one stung.
It was meant to. A budget you write in January and never open again is a wish.

title: The number at the bottom
setting: Sales have grown and the owner cannot feel the difference.

lines.t: Revenue is up 18% on last year.
And the bottom line?
Almost exactly where it was.
Then your profit margin has fallen. You're selling more and keeping less of it.
Turnover is what people ask about at conferences.
Turnover is what you tell them. The bottom line is what you take home.
When do we break even on the new branch?
The break-even point is 340 covers a month. You're at 290.
So it's in the red.
Fifty covers away from being in the black, which is two more tables a day.
That sounds achievable when you put it like that.
It's the same number I've been writing down since November. Today it fitted on one line.

title: The one that will never pay
setting: An old unpaid invoice is making the accounts look healthier than they are.

lines.t: The invoice from that company in Ruse is fourteen months old.
They closed in March.
Then we write it off. It sits in accounts receivable making everything look better than it is.
How much?
Four thousand two hundred.
Write it off this quarter, so the income statement tells the truth.
And the balance sheet?
Cleaner without it. What's sitting in accounts payable?
Eleven suppliers, all within terms.
Keep it that way. A company that pays on time gets answered on time.

title: Sixty days, they said
setting: A good client who has never once paid on schedule.

lines.t: This invoice is ninety days overdue.
Their payment terms say sixty.
Which they agreed to and have never once met.
Do I chase the invoice again?
Somebody chases it every week. Change the arrangement instead of the reminder.
Meaning what?
Upfront payment of 30% on the next job, or a deposit before we order materials.
They'll try to bargain me down. They always do.
Then build the discount into the quote so you have something to give away.
And if they ask for a refund on the last job?
They won't. They're slow payers who like the work.
Slow costs us the interest on the money we borrowed to do their work.

title: Borrow or sell
setting: Two hundred thousand is needed and there are only two ways to get it.

lines.t: To open the second site I need two hundred thousand.
Borrow it, or sell part of the company. Those are the two doors.
What's the interest rate now?
Around 8%. The loan is repaid over five years and the debt sits on your balance sheet the whole time.
And the other door?
You give away equity. No repayments, and a shareholder who expects a dividend and a say.
I'd rather owe a bank than explain myself at a meeting.
Then borrow, and leave your working capital alone. That's the money that pays wages in a slow month.
What's the return on investment on the second site?
On your numbers, 22 months. On mine, three years.
Why the difference?
You counted the first site as a cash cow that funds the second, and it has been quietly slowing since spring.
The audit starts on the 14th.
Which quarter are they looking at?
All four. It's the whole fiscal year.
Then I want everything in one folder by Friday.
The forecast for next year as well?
They won't ask for it. I want it anyway, while the numbers are still in my head.
Year on year we're up in three months and down in nine.
That's the sentence that goes at the top of the report.
Nobody reads past the first page.
Which is why the first page should hold the thing you'd least like to explain.

title: Keep the receipt
setting: An expense claim arrives with more items than receipts.

lines.t: Your expense claim has eleven items and four receipts.
The rest were card payments. It's all on the statement.
A statement shows the amount. It doesn't show what you bought or the VAT on it.
Is a lunch tax-deductible?
With a client, sometimes. Alone in an airport, no.
That's the one I was hoping about.
Everybody hopes about that one.
When is the tax return due?
The 31st, and I'd like your receipts three weeks before that rather than the night before.
And payroll?
Payroll runs on the 25th whatever else is happening. That date has never moved in nine years.
